items.title: [ScienceDaily] A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics
items.content_html: Scientists have spotted hints of a mysterious rotation in the universe’s oldest light that could reveal new physics and shed light on dark matter and dark energy. A new technique developed at UC San Diego could help rule out misleading telescope errors, bringing researchers closer to determining whether the strange signal is real.

items.title: [phys.org] Researchers urge protection of ocean climate refugia as warming intensifies
items.content_html: A review of marine research argues that conservation plans should include ocean climate refugia—areas where conditions help species withstand climate change—as warming, acidification, oxygen loss and other pressures reshape marine ecosystems. Researchers reviewed 798 studies published from 2021 to 2026 and selected 82 that identified or mapped refugia. They found three main approaches: measuring low climate exposure, observing ecological resilience and predicting future habitat suitability. The authors say refugia could guide the designation of marine protected areas and restoration efforts, but substantial research gaps remain in the high seas and deep ocean. Identifying such areas could also help countries plan a network of protected areas under the U.N. High Seas Treaty, which is now in force, they say.

items.title: [Nautilus] There’s New Hope for Detecting Alzheimer’s Before Cognitive Deficits Manifest
items.content_html:
With no cure for Alzheimer’s on the horizon, and our best treatments only slowing the progression of the disease, there’s been an intense effort to find earlier means of detection. Now, a new study published in Neuroimage Reports is offering hope of diagnosis even before cognitive symptoms become noticeable.   

A team of biomedical imaging specialists, pathologists, and neuroscientists from Johns Hopkins University studied how the brains of older adults changed over time by analyzing hundreds of MRI scans and PET scans. They relied on longitudinal data from two different studies (the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline Among Normal Individuals study) that included people from across the Alzheimer’s spectrum, from cognitively healthy to full-blown dementia.

Read more: “How the Brain’s Failing Trash Compactor Can Contribute to Alzheimer’s Disease”

items.title: [reddit.com] Black hole ringdowns provide a new test of Einstein's relativity
items.content_html: Using computer models and a review of existing research, a team of more than 70 researchers found that post-merger “ringdown” signals from hundreds of observed black hole collisions match predictions of Einstein’s general relativity. The study, published in *Classical and Quantum Gravity*, examines black hole spectroscopy, which tests a newly merged black hole by measuring the gravitational waves it produces as it settles. The researchers said current observations limit measurement precision, while next-generation ground-based detectors could enable more detailed tests. Study co-author Gregorio Carullo, a University of Birmingham physicist, said the method could help investigate gravity and possible new forms of matter and energy.

items.title: [scientificamerican.com] Neanderthal DNA variant linked to smaller visual brain region, lower schizophrenia odds
items.content_html: Researchers report that a Neanderthal-derived DNA variant is associated with a smaller occipital lobe and lower odds of schizophrenia in modern humans. In UK Biobank data, each copy of the variant corresponded to about 0.85 cubic centimeters less occipital-lobe volume; people with two copies had nearly 10% lower odds of schizophrenia than those with no copies. The occipital lobe processes visual information. The variant lies near DAAM1, a gene involved in brain development, but researchers have not established how it affects the brain or whether the smaller lobe explains the schizophrenia association. The variant was not associated with a meaningful difference in intelligence, and outside researchers cautioned against drawing conclusions about Neanderthal brain function from the findings in modern humans. The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Its authors say further work, including studies using brain organoids or animal models, could investigate the mechanism.

items.title: [sciencealert.com] Florida researchers identify mushroom with psychedelic and deadly toxins
items.content_html: Researchers identified Galerina indica as the first known mushroom to contain both psilocybin, which produces psychedelic effects, and amatoxins, which are linked to fatal mushroom poisonings. The team confirmed the compounds through chemical analysis and genome sequencing after finding specimens in Florida wetlands. The species stains blue when handled, a feature associated with psilocybin that could mislead foragers into assuming it is safe. Researchers said toxin levels in G. indica have not been established. They also found evidence of rare gene transfers in the mushroom’s evolutionary history. Future experiments could disable genes that produce either compound to test their roles in the fungus, the researchers said.

items.title: [sciencealert.com] Studies explore how ancient gases may have formed pure sulfur deposits on Mars
items.content_html: NASA’s Curiosity rover discovered pure elemental sulfur crystals in rocks that broke beneath its wheels in Mars’ Gediz Vallis channel in 2024, the first confirmed discovery of sulfur in that form on the planet. Similar rocks covered about 2,100 square meters, and a study published in June 2026 estimated that the deposit formed between 3.1 billion and 2.8 billion years ago. Researchers propose that sulfur-bearing gases from ancient volcanic activity became trapped underground and later escaped as erosion exposed the deposits. A separate experiment found that dissolved sulfide and chlorate could react in acidic water at room temperature to produce elemental sulfur without high heat or life.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
items.content_html: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud. These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining for valuable metals.

items.title: [sciencealert.com] Astronomers trace disappearing exoplanet to an unseen planetary neighbor
items.content_html: Astronomers say the giant exoplanet TOI-2535 b stopped transiting its star because an unseen companion’s gravity caused its orbit to tilt and wobble, taking it out of Earth’s line of sight. The planet, about 1,100 light-years away, still orbits its star; researchers tracked its transits for seven years before they vanished in March 2026. Astronomers have not observed the companion directly, but changes in the timing and shape of TOI-2535 b’s transits point to a second giant planet, possibly at least as massive as Saturn. The pair’s orbital interaction is unusually strong, and the cause of their tilted orbits remains unclear. Researchers expect TOI-2535 b’s transits to become visible again in 30 to 50 years, while the companion could appear sooner.

items.title: [discovermagazine.com] 6,000-year-old tooth tracks dietary shift as farming reached Denmark
items.content_html: A tooth from Rødhals Man, a hunter-gatherer buried on Denmark’s Sejerø island nearly 6,000 years ago, records a shift from seafood in childhood toward more land-based food in adolescence and adulthood as farming reached the islands. Researchers used chemical signatures in successive layers of a premolar to reconstruct his dietary changes. They say the evidence makes him one of the rare individuals known to have lived through the transition. His ancestry was that of the local forager population, while his diet suggests contact with the incoming farming way of life. The chemistry cannot establish whether his land-based food came directly from farms. But researchers favor food from, or proximity to, farming communities because his diet lacked the freshwater fish typical of inland foragers.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study
items.content_html: Scientists have uncovered a surprising genetic connection to spinal degeneration and found that an existing osteoporosis drug can prevent damaging mineral buildup in zebrafish spines. The discovery could pave the way for new treatments that slow or prevent a major cause of chronic back pain.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] NASA warns this year's Monster El Niño could be even bigger than legendary 1997 event
items.content_html: NASA scientists warn that the rapidly intensifying 2026 El Niño could surpass the historic 1997-98 event, which triggered devastating weather extremes around the world. Satellite data reveal striking similarities between the two, raising the possibility of major rainfall and flooding this winter, although the exact impacts remain uncertain.

items.title: [thehindu.com] SpaceX's orbital catch leaves experts seeking proof of repeatable reuse
items.content_html: Aerospace specialists say SpaceX must show that its Starship spacecraft can survive repeated atmospheric returns and be prepared for another flight to demonstrate reliable reuse. In the Texas test, the company caught Starship’s upper stage after an orbital flight for the first time. SpaceX said the spacecraft’s systems, including its heat shield, appeared to work well, but experts cautioned that a single recovery does not show the vehicle is ready for sensitive payloads or missions. Catching Starship was more demanding than catching the lower booster because the spacecraft returns from a higher altitude and at greater speed. Aerospace engineer Alistair John of the University of Sheffield said the heat shield and engines need to be checked for damage, while aerospace analyst Kathleen Curlee of Georgetown University said repeated successes are needed to demonstrate mission readiness. NASA plans to use a Starship variant as a lunar lander. The agency is preparing an Artemis mission in which four astronauts are expected to practice docking with lunar landers in orbit; it is targeting Artemis IV for a lunar landing as soon as 2028.

items.title: 🔓 [WIRED] New Species of Giant Fungus Discovered in China Grows up to 20 Inches Tall
items.content_html: Sometimes new species evade detection because they’re tiny and thus easy to miss—not this giant fungus. items.title: [ScienceDaily] Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
items.content_html: Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a powerful new way to identify people at risk.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Physicists use laser light to unlock a crystal's hidden electrical powers
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered how to use flashes of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions inside a crystal, solving a decades-old mystery about how the material behaves. The laser-induced alignment lasts just a trillionth of a second, but the breakthrough could open the door to new ways of processing and storing information.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
items.content_html: Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.

items.title: [space.com] Apollo 12 lightning strikes prompted NASA to tighten launch weather rules
items.content_html: Lightning struck NASA’s Apollo 12 Saturn V rocket twice within seconds of its Nov. 14, 1969, launch, disrupting spacecraft telemetry and endangering the mission. Mission Control engineer John Aaron recognized the readings from an earlier test and recommended switching the Signal Conditioning Equipment to its auxiliary setting, which restored the data. Investigators concluded the rocket and its conductive exhaust plume had triggered a discharge in an electrically charged part of the atmosphere, even though no active thunderstorm lay along the immediate flight path. NASA expanded launch weather restrictions to account for atmospheric electrical conditions, not only visible lightning and thunderstorms.

items.title: [newspaceeconomy.ca] NASA identifies potential biosignature in Mars rock sample
items.content_html: Researchers are investigating Mars, Jupiter’s icy moons and other solar-system sites as possible habitats, but Earth remains the only world known to support life. NASA’s Perseverance rover collected a rock sample in July 2024 that the agency later described as containing a potential biosignature: organic material and mineral patterns that could reflect microbial activity but also have possible nonbiological explanations. Mars preserves evidence of ancient surface water, while Europa and Enceladus may hold oceans beneath ice. Habitable conditions do not establish that organisms exist; water, usable energy and accessible chemical ingredients must come together over time. NASA’s Europa Clipper and the European Space Agency’s JUICE mission are traveling to study Jupiter’s icy moons, where possible exchanges between surface and subsurface reservoirs also raise planetary-protection concerns.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps
items.content_html: Scientists have captured electrons making seemingly impossible jumps across forbidden energy gaps in graphene, with some transitions occurring at a remarkable 100% probability. The breakthrough offers an unprecedented look at quantum behavior and could help unlock a new generation of ultrafast, light-controlled electronics.

items.title: [c-jcm.com] Cancer AI studies report support benefits, high accuracy and readability gaps
items.content_html: A study of 140 patients with pancreatic cancer found that those who used an AI assistant’s psychological-support feature had lower anxiety and quality-of-life scores than nonusers. More frequent overall use was also associated with lower anxiety, but the relationship was borderline statistically significant. Researchers assessed patients once in April and May 2026; the findings show an association, not that the tool caused the differences. Separate lung-cancer research found high accuracy in AI answers to patient questions, but all three systems tested produced text at a 10th- to 12th-grade reading level. Other cancer studies presented for a pathology meeting reported on AI applications for classifying tumors, drafting molecular reports and deciding when rapid testing could be deferred.
